info.name: Dynamic Alarm: App
info.description:
Every endpoint the mobile app calls, in the order onboarding uses them.

Run the folders top to bottom the first time. Everything destructive lives in the final Cleanup folder, so a straight run creates a working schedule and only then tears it down. `Register device` stores the bearer token in a collection variable and every later request picks it up automatically, so nothing needs to be pasted by hand. Creating the two places and the routine stores their ids the same way, which is what the schedule request needs.

Every response is wrapped in `{ "success": true, "data": ... }` or `{ "success": false, "error": { code, message, details } }`. The shapes are declared in `packages/types/src/api.ts`, and the API is compiled against them, so what is documented here and what the server sends cannot drift.

Onboarding uses `POST /plan/options` rather than `/plan/preview`: it shows the traveller three journeys and stores the chosen index as the schedule's `journeyOffset`. The preview remains for a single answer.

Endpoints the app never calls live in the companion collection, `Dynamic Alarm: Backend`.

item.name: 1. Device

request.description:
The only unauthenticated endpoint, because it is what creates the credential every other route requires.

The token comes back once and is never shown again: only its SHA-256 hash is stored. If the app loses it, the device cannot be recovered and must register afresh, which is the trade for a database dump not handing over every device's identity.

Response: `RegisterDeviceResponse` ({ deviceId, token }).

response.name: error: validation

request.description:
The mutable facts about a device. Platform is not one of them.

`pushToken` is nullable, not merely optional, and the difference matters: omitting it means unchanged, sending `null` means notification permission was revoked. Collapsing the two would leave the server pushing at a token the device no longer has.

Response: `DeviceResponse` ({ deviceId, platform, timezone, hasPushToken }). The push token comes back as a boolean, because the device already holds the value; what it cannot otherwise learn is whether the server still has one.

item.description: The anonymous account. There is no sign-in: the app registers on first launch and keeps the token in expo-secure-store.

item.name: 2. Places

request.description:
Dutch address, station and POI search, proxied so the NS key never reaches the app bundle.

Authenticated like everything else. An open proxy to a key with a shared ceiling of 300 requests per 5 minutes is a way for anyone to switch off journey planning for every user.

`q` must be at least 3 characters, enforced here rather than trusted to the client, because this is the one route a user can fire per keystroke. The app must debounce as well.

Response: `PlaceAutosuggestResponse` (PlaceSuggestion[]). Stations carry `nsStationCode`, addresses do not.

exec: pm.test('lat comes back as a number, not a MySQL decimal string', function () {

request.description:
Coordinates rather than a station. Journeys are planned door to door, and storing a station would throw away the walk to it.

Latitude and longitude are bounded to the Netherlands plus a margin. A pair that passes a plain range check can still be in the Atlantic, and that failure surfaces as an NS call that finds nothing followed by an alarm the app cannot explain.

Response: `PlaceResponse` (Place).
The destination half of the commute. Stored so the schedule can name it.

This device's places, oldest first.

Response: `ListPlacesResponse` (Place[]).

Another device's place id answers 404, not 403. The device id is part of the lookup rather than checked after it, so a real id and an invented one are indistinguishable. A 403 would confirm which place ids exist to anyone holding any token.
Every field optional. Sending only `label` leaves the coordinates alone.

item.description: Saved origins and destinations, and the address search that produces them.

item.name: 3. Routines

request.description:
Steps carry no `order` field. Position in the array is the order, because two sources for one fact means something has to break the tie when they disagree, and the user reads that as the app losing the arrangement they just made.

Disabled steps are kept and contribute zero minutes. That is how "I'll skip breakfast today" works without making the user retype it tomorrow. The example above totals 33 minutes, not 78.

Response: `RoutineResponse` (Routine, steps included).
Response: `ListRoutinesResponse` (Routine[]), steps sorted by their stored order.

Sending `steps` replaces the list entirely. Omitting it leaves the steps untouched, so renaming a routine does not mean sending them all back.

Replacement rather than a diff, because the editor renames, reorders and deletes at once, and working out which of those happened from a set of ids is guesswork that gets the order wrong. Step ids therefore change on every edit; nothing references them, since the engine reads minutes rather than identity.

item.description: The morning routine, whose enabled steps sum to the time between the alarm and leaving the house.

item.name: 4. Schedules

exec: pm.test('arrivalTime is HH:mm, not the MySQL TIME', function () {

request.description:
`arrivalTime` is wall-clock, not an instant. "Be at work by 08:30" stays 08:30 across daylight saving, which a stored timestamp would not.

`daysOfWeek` uses ISO numbering, 1 is Monday. Duplicates are rejected: the same day twice would arm two occurrences for one morning and ring twice.

`mode` is `PUBLIC_TRANSPORT`, `CAR` or `FIXED`. `FIXED` also requires `fixedTravelMinutes`, since there is no provider to ask and without that number no wake time can be computed at all.

The four buffers sit at different layers of the calculation and a single combined buffer cannot express that. `transferMinutes` in particular is never subtracted: it is handed to the NS planner as a minimum connection time, so a transfer that tight is never proposed in the first place.

Every referenced place and routine must belong to this device, checked explicitly. The foreign keys accept any valid id, so without that check a device could point a schedule at another device's place and read back where that person lives through the plan preview.

Response: `ScheduleResponse` (Schedule).

`originAccess` and `destinationAccess` are how the traveller reaches each station, and they are separate because the usual Dutch commute is a bike at the home end and a walk at the other. One setting for both would get one of them wrong, and on a two-kilometre access leg the difference is around twenty minutes applied straight to the wake-up time. Only `WALK` and `BIKE` exist: driving to a station is a real habit, but the parking and the walk from the car park are unmodelled, so a car access leg would be optimistic in exactly the direction that makes someone miss a train.

Both are ignored when `mode` is not `PUBLIC_TRANSPORT`, which is the only mode with a station to reach.

`journeyOffset` is which on-time journey to take, counting back from the latest departure. Zero is the most sleep and is what the engine picks unasked. It is a **position, not a train**: the alarm recurs and the timetable does not hold still, so a cancellation moves the choice along the list rather than invalidating it. A morning with fewer options clamps to the earliest rather than refusing to plan. Get the value from `POST /plan/options`, where it is the index.
Response: `ListSchedulesResponse` (Schedule[]).

Paused rather than deleted, so a holiday does not lose the setup.

Coherence is checked against the merged result rather than the payload: switching to `FIXED` without sending a duration, or clearing the duration while already on `FIXED`, both leave a schedule that cannot compute a wake time, and neither is visible from the request alone.

Every field from create is patchable here too, including `originAccess`, `destinationAccess` and `journeyOffset`.

item.description: A recurring commitment: be at this place, by this time, on these days. Note what is absent, there is no wake-up time here. The user does not own that number.

item.name: 5. Plan

exec: pm.test('returns at least one option', function () {
const sorted = departures.slice().sort(function (a, b) { return b - a; });
// The index is what a schedule stores, so read it from here.

request.description:
The same commute planned several ways, so the traveller can choose.

Same body as the preview. The engine's own answer is the latest journey that still arrives on time, because that buys the most sleep, and it is the wrong answer for anyone who wants a seat, the direct train, or simply some margin.

Returns up to three whole `WakePlan` objects rather than a list of departures: the number being chosen between is the wake-up time, and that only exists once the routine and the buffers have been applied.

**Ordered latest departure first, and the index is the `journeyOffset` to store on the schedule.** That ordering is part of the contract, not presentation.

Costs the same NS budget as one preview: a single request already returns several itineraries.

When nothing arrives on time it returns a single plan for the least-late journey, carrying `feasible: false` and `shortfallMinutes`, because the user still needs an alarm.

Response: `PlanOptionsResponse` (WakePlan[]).

exec: pm.test('no journey departs in the past', function () {

request.description:
A wake plan computed and thrown away. This is what makes onboarding honest: the user is still deciding, and the only convincing answer is their real commute against the real timetable.

Takes coordinates rather than saved places, because at this point nothing is saved.

POST despite reading nothing. The body carries two coordinate pairs and a routine length, which is where the user lives and works. In a query string that lands in access logs and browser history.

`date` is optional. Omitted, it means the next time that clock reading comes round, which is tomorrow once today's has passed.

An infeasible result is still a 200. "The earliest you can arrive is 08:41" is an answer, not a failure, so the plan carries `feasible: false` and `shortfallMinutes`, and the alarm is still set for that best effort.

Response: `PlanPreviewResponse` (WakePlan). `breakdown` carries every term of the calculation, so the app can show its work and "why did it wake me at 06:12?" stays answerable.

`originAccess` and `destinationAccess` default to `WALK` when omitted, so an older client keeps the behaviour it was written against. Sending `BIKE` for the home end is the common case and typically moves the wake time later by ten to twenty minutes for the same train.

request.description:
One leg, no transfers, and a continuous risk buffer rather than a discrete one: traffic is a distribution, while a train is caught or missed.

For a future arrival TomTom uses predictive traffic only and ignores the live picture, so a plan made the night before is a forecast. The monitor re-queries as departure approaches, and the engine tightens the buffer once inside the live window.

No provider is called, so `journey` is null and the coordinates are only carried for symmetry. Useful for checking the engine without spending NS budget, and the fallback when someone travels a way neither provider models.

`date` is pinned here to show the parameter; the pre-request script sets it to tomorrow.

item.description: The engine, run against live NS and TomTom data.

item.name: 6. Occurrences (M2, not built yet)

request.description:
The next armed occurrence, carrying both wake times.

`anchorWakeAt` is the pessimistic time computed at arming, and it is what the device actually schedules as a local exact alarm. `currentWakeAt` is the latest computed time. The alarm only ever moves later, so a dropped push, airplane mode or a dead backend means waking at the anchor, slightly early, and still making it.
Sent once the device's local alarm actually matches `currentWakeAt`. Without it the server cannot tell "pushed" from "armed", and would re-push the same change forever.
Why the alarm moved, in order. Not optional bookkeeping: without a written trail, "why did it wake me at 06:12?" is undebuggable.

item.description: One day's instance of a schedule, and the audit trail behind every alarm change. These routes are declared in `API_ENDPOINTS` and will 404 until the monitor loop lands in M2. They are here so the shape is agreed before the app is written against it.

item.name: 7. Cleanup
item.description:
Last on purpose. These used to sit in their own resource folders, which broke the instruction to run the collection top to bottom: the places and the routine were deleted before the schedule that references them was created, and every schedule request after that failed on an id that was never set.

Order matters here too. A place or a routine still referenced by a schedule answers 409 and names what is in the way, so the schedule goes first.

request.description: 204, or 409 while a schedule still uses it.

204 on success, and 409 while a schedule still points at it, naming the schedules in the way.

The foreign key would refuse this anyway, but as a driver error it reaches the user as "something went wrong". The check exists to turn that into a sentence they can act on.
The other half of the commute, so a full run leaves nothing behind.
